# Introduction

The testing procedures implemented in **TestCQS** require the spectral
representation of the null covariance (or scale) structure.
Rather than specifying the covariance matrix directly, every commutative
quadratic subspace is represented by

- an orthogonal basis matrix `H`,
- a vector `qq` containing the multiplicities of the distinct eigenvalues.

The package provides a large collection of `basis_*()` functions that
construct these objects automatically for many commonly used covariance
structures.

This vignette describes the available basis generators and illustrates
their use.

```r
library(TestCQS)
```


# Notation and construction principles

Throughout this vignette we use the following notation.

| Symbol | Description |
|:-------|:------------|
| \(\otimes\) | Kronecker product. |
| \(q\) | Dimension of an ordinary multivariate observation. |
| \(p\) | Number of blocks in a doubly multivariate model. |
| \(m\) | Dimension of each block in a doubly multivariate model. |
| \(\mathbf 1_q\) | \(q\)-dimensional vector of ones. | 
| \(\mathbf I_q\) | Identity matrix of order \(q\). |
| \(\mathbf J_q\) | Matrix of ones of order \(q\times q\). |
| \(\mathbf 0_q\) | Zero matrix of order \(q\times q\). |
| \(\mathbf e_{i,q}\) | The \(i\)-th canonical basis vector of \(\mathbb R^q\). |
| \(\mathbf E_{ij}\) | \(m\times m\) matrix having a single 1 in position \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) and zeros elsewhere. |
| \(\mathbf P_{1_q}=\tfrac1q\mathbf J_q\) | Orthogonal projection onto the subspace spanned by the vector of ones \(\mathbf 1_q\). |
| \(\mathbf Q_{1_q}=\mathbf I_q-\mathbf P_{1_q}\) | Orthogonal projection onto the orthogonal complement of the vector of ones \(\mathbf 1_q\). |

The testing procedures implemented in `TestCQS` are based on the
spectral decomposition of covariance matrices. Consequently, every basis
generator returns

- an orthogonal basis matrix `H`, whose columns span the
  eigenspaces corresponding to equal eigenvalues,
- a vector `qq` containing the multiplicities of these eigenspaces.

For the ordinary multivariate covariance structures we denote the basis
matrices by

| Covariance structure | Basis matrix | Generator |
|:---------------------|:-------------|:----------|
| Sphericity | \(\mathbf H_{S,q}=\mathbf I_q\) | `basis_S(q)` |
| Diagonality | \(\mathbf H_{D,q}=\mathbf I_q\) | `basis_D(q)` |
| Compound symmetry | \(\mathbf H_{CS,q}\) | `basis_CS(q)` |
| Circular Toeplitz | \(\mathbf H_{CT,q}\) | `basis_CT(q)` |

Here, \(\mathbf H_{CS,q}\) and \(\mathbf H_{CT,q}\) denote the ordinary
compound symmetry and circular Toeplitz basis matrices of dimension
\(q\), respectively, as defined in the *Ordinary multivariate structures* section.

Notice that the basis matrices for sphericity and diagonality are both equal to the identity matrix. Nevertheless, we distinguish the notation \(\mathbf H_{S,q}\) and \(\mathbf H_{D,q}\) because they correspond to different covariance structures and play different roles in the construction of
doubly multivariate covariance models.


# The output of basis generators

Every basis generator returns the same type of object.

```r
obj <- basis_CS(5)

names(obj)
```

The returned list contains

- `H` – an orthogonal matrix whose columns are arranged according to  groups of equal eigenvalues,

- `qq` – a vector of eigenvalue multiplicities.

For example,

```r
obj$qq
```

indicates that the first eigenvalue has multiplicity one, whereas the second eigenvalue has multiplicity four.

The dimensions satisfy

```r
dim(obj$H)
sum(obj$qq)
```

where the number of columns of `H` always equals the sum of the multiplicities.

The objects returned by every `basis_*()` function can be supplied directly
to `runTestCQS()`. For the built-in covariance structures this is optional,
since `runTestCQS()` generates the basis automatically from the structure
name. Nevertheless, the following two calls are equivalent.

```r
obj <- basis_CS(6)

res1 <- runTestCQS(X, q = 6, H = "CS")
res2 <- runTestCQS(X, H = obj$H, qq = obj$qq)
```

The explicit representation is particularly useful when constructing
user-defined commutative quadratic subspaces or when inspecting the basis
matrices returned by the package.


# Ordinary multivariate structures

For an ordinary multivariate model the covariance matrix has dimension \(q \times q\). The package implements four commonly used covariance structures.

|Structure|Generator|
|:---------|:----------------|
|Sphericity|`basis_S(q)`|
|Diagonality|`basis_D(q)`|
|Compound symmetry|`basis_CS(q)`|
|Circular Toeplitz|`basis_CT(q)`|


## Sphericity

The sphericity structure assumes that all variables have the same variance
and are mutually uncorrelated. Consequently, the covariance matrix is a
multiple of the identity matrix,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}\lambda & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
                                 0 & \lambda & \cdots & 0 \\
                                 \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
                                 0 & 0 & \cdots & \lambda 
                      \end{smallmatrix}\right) = \lambda \mathbf I_q.
\]

Since all eigenvalues are equal, the covariance matrix possesses only one
distinct eigenvalue, with multiplicity \(q\). Any orthogonal matrix may therefore serve
as the matrix of eigenvectors. The package uses the identity
matrix as the default orthogonal basis.

```r
obj <- basis_S(6)

obj$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 6
```

indicating that the single eigenvalue has multiplicity six.

The corresponding basis matrix \(\mathbf H_{S,q}\), is obtained by

```r
obj$H
```

and, for the sphericity structure, is simply the identity matrix (\mathbf I_q).

**Statistical interpretation:** The sphericity structure represents an
isotropic covariance model. All variables have the same variance and
there is no covariance between distinct variables. Consequently,
variability is the same in every direction of the variable space, and the
covariance matrix is proportional to the identity matrix.

Sphericity often serves as a benchmark or null model in multivariate
analysis. Testing sphericity can be used to assess whether the covariance
matrix is compatible with an isotropic structure or whether a more
general covariance model is required.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Reference model in multivariate hypothesis testing.
> - Isotropic measurement-error models.
> - Situations in which no direction in the variable space is assumed to
    have a different variability from any other direction.


## Diagonality

Under the diagonal covariance structure,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
                                                0 & \lambda_2 & \cdots & 0 \\
                                                \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
                                                0 & 0 & \cdots & \lambda_q
                      \end{smallmatrix}\right) = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_q),
\]

the variables are mutually uncorrelated, while each variable may have a
different variance.

In the generic case where the diagonal elements are distinct, the
covariance matrix has \(q\) distinct eigenvalues, each with multiplicity
one. Consequently,

```r
basis_D(6)$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 1 1 1 1 1 1
```

The corresponding orthogonal basis \(\mathbf H_{D,q}\) is the identity matrix \(\mathbf I_q\).
In this case, each coordinate axis forms a one-dimensional eigenspace.
The columns of \(\mathbf H_{D,q}\) therefore correspond directly to the
individual variables.

**Statistical interpretation:** A diagonal covariance matrix assumes that
the variables are uncorrelated, while allowing each variable to have its
own variance. Thus, unlike the sphericity structure, diagonality does not
impose a common variance across variables.

The diagonal structure is useful when the variables are believed to be
uncorrelated but may exhibit substantially different levels of
variability. It can also serve as an intermediate model between the fully
unstructured covariance matrix and the more restrictive sphericity
structure.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Variables measured on different scales but assumed to be uncorrelated.
> - Preliminary model assessment before introducing a more complex covariance structure.
> - Testing whether the off-diagonal covariance terms can be neglected
    without imposing the additional equal-variance assumption of sphericity.


## Compound symmetry

Under the compound symmetry (CS) structure, all variables have the same
variance and every pair of distinct variables has the same covariance.
Consequently, the covariance matrix has the form

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} \sigma^2 & \sigma^2\rho & \cdots & \sigma^2\rho \\
                                                \sigma^2\rho & \sigma^2 & \cdots & \sigma^2\rho \\
                                                \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
                                                \sigma^2\rho & \sigma^2\rho & \cdots & \sigma^2
                      \end{smallmatrix}\right) = \sigma^2(1-\rho)\mathbf I_q + \sigma^2\rho\mathbf J_q.
\]

The parameter \(\sigma^2\) represents the common variance of all variables, while \(\rho\) represents the correlation between every pair of distinct variables.

While the parametrization by \(\sigma^2\) and \(\rho\) is commonly used in multivariate statistics, since it provides a direct statistical interpretation of the parameters, `TestCQS` works with the spectral decomposition of the covariance matrix. Using the orthogonal projections \(\mathbf P_q\) and \(\mathbf Q_q\) introduced in the notation section, the compound symmetry covariance matrix can be written as

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \lambda_1\mathbf P_{1_q} + \lambda_2\mathbf Q_{1_q}.
\]

The connection between the two parametrizations is

\[
\lambda_1=\sigma^2(1+(q-1)\rho), \qquad \lambda_2=\sigma^2(1-\rho).
\]

Thus, in the generic case \(\rho\neq 0\), the compound symmetry structure has two distinct eigenvalues:

- \(\lambda_1\) with multiplicity \(1\),
- \(\lambda_2\) with multiplicity \(q-1\).

The multiplicities are obtained from the basis generator by

```r
obj <- basis_CS(6)

obj$qq
```

which returns

```
[1] 1 5
```

The basis matrix returned by `basis_CS(q)` contains the corresponding
eigenvectors ordered according to these multiplicities. Its first column is
the normalized constant vector \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{q}}\mathbf 1_q\), as can
be verified by

```r
round(obj$H[, 1], 3)
```

This vector spans the one-dimensional eigenspace associated with
\(\lambda_1\). The remaining \(q-1\) columns form an orthonormal basis of the eigenspace associated with (\lambda_2), which is the subspace orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_q\).

Consequently, the basis matrix can be represented as

\[
\mathbf H_{CS,q}=\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{q}}\mathbf 1_q: \widetilde{\mathbf Q}\right),
\]

where \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\) is a \(q\times q-1\) matrix whose columns form any orthonormal basis of the subspace orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_q\).

The particular choice of \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\) is not unique. Any
orthonormal basis of this subspace gives a valid spectral basis. The
generator `basis_CS(q)` provides one particular orthonormal choice.


**Statistical interpretation:** Compound symmetry assumes that all variables have equal variances and that every pair of variables has the same covariance. Consequently, the variables
are exchangeable, meaning that no variable plays a distinguished role.

From the spectral perspective, the total variability is decomposed into two
orthogonal components:

- variation in the overall mean direction, represented by \(\mathbf P_{1_q}\), and
- variation orthogonal to the mean direction, represented by \(\mathbf Q_{1_q}\).

This decomposition explains why only two distinct eigenvalues are required to
describe the entire covariance structure.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Repeated-measures experiments in which all measurement occasions have the same variance and the        same pairwise covariance.
> - Balanced experimental designs where treatment levels are considered exchangeable.
> - Clustered or grouped observations exhibiting homogeneous within-cluster dependence.


## Circular Toeplitz

A circular Toeplitz (CT) covariance matrix is completely determined by its
first row,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathrm{CT}}
=
\operatorname{Toep}(\tau_0,\tau_1,\tau_2,\tau_{\lfloor q/2\rfloor},
\tau_{\lfloor q/2\rfloor-1},\ldots,\tau_2,\tau_1),
\]

or, equivalently,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor q/2\rfloor}\tau_i\,\mathbf{SC}(q,i),
\]

where \(\mathbf{SC}(q,i)\) denotes the symmetric circular matrix having ones
at circular distance \(i\) and zeros elsewhere. Thus,
\(\mathbf{SC}(q,i)\) contains ones on the \(i\)-th super- and
sub-diagonals, with the entries continuing across the boundaries by
wrap-around. For example, the circular Toeplitz matrices for \(q=5\) and \(q=6\) have the forms

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} \tau_0 & \tau_1 & \tau_2 & \tau_2 & \tau_1 \\
                                                \tau_1 & \tau_0 & \tau_1 & \tau_2 & \tau_2 \\
                                                \tau_2 & \tau_1 & \tau_0 & \tau_1 & \tau_2 \\
                                                \tau_2 & \tau_2 & \tau_1 & \tau_0 & \tau_1 \\
                                                \tau_1 & \tau_2 & \tau_2 & \tau_1 & \tau_0
                      \end{smallmatrix}\right), \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} \tau_0 & \tau_1 & \tau_2 & \tau_3 & \tau_2 & \tau_1 \\
                                                \tau_1 & \tau_0 & \tau_1 & \tau_2 & \tau_3 & \tau_2 \\
                                                \tau_2 & \tau_1 & \tau_0 & \tau_1 & \tau_2 & \tau_3 \\
                                                \tau_3 & \tau_2 & \tau_1 & \tau_0 & \tau_1 & \tau_2 \\
                                                \tau_2 & \tau_3 & \tau_2 & \tau_1 & \tau_0 & \tau_1 \\
                                                \tau_1 & \tau_2 & \tau_3 & \tau_2 & \tau_1 & \tau_0
                      \end{smallmatrix}\right).
\]

Unlike an ordinary Toeplitz matrix, the first row is obtained from the last
row by a circular shift. Consequently, every row is simply a cyclic shift of
the preceding one.

Although this representation provides an intuitive interpretation of the
covariance parameters \(\tau_0,\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_{\lfloor q/2\rfloor}\), `TestCQS` is based on the
spectral representation of the covariance matrix.

A fundamental property of
the circular Toeplitz structure is that every circular Toeplitz covariance
matrix of the same dimension shares the same orthonormal
eigenvectors. Only the corresponding eigenvalues depend on the particular covariance
parameters.

Although the individual eigenvectors within a multiple-eigenvalue
eigenspace are not unique, `TestCQS` uses a fixed orthonormal basis obtained
from the real Fourier representation. Specifically, let

\[
\mathbf H_{CT,q}=(t_{ij}), \qquad t_{ij} = q^{-1/2}\left[\cos\left(\tfrac{2\pi ij}{q}\right)
+ \sin\left(\tfrac{2\pi ij}{q}\right)\right].
\]

The matrix returned by `basis_CT(q)` is obtained from these Fourier
eigenvectors by a specific permutation of their columns. The first column
is retained as the first column. The remaining columns are then arranged
symmetrically from the two ends of the original Fourier basis: the second
column is followed by the last column, the third column by the
next-to-last column, and so on.

Thus, the columns of the returned basis are ordered as

\[
1,\;2,\;q,\;3,\;q-1,\;4,\;q-2,\;\ldots.
\]

This ordering is chosen so that columns corresponding to the same
eigenvalue occur consecutively. It therefore makes the eigenspace
multiplicities particularly transparent in the vector `qq`.

For odd \(q\), the ordering terminates with the two central columns

\[
\tfrac{q+1}{2} = \left\lfloor\frac q2\right\rfloor+1,\qquad\tfrac{q+3}{2} =
\left\lfloor\tfrac q2\right\rfloor+2.
\]

Consequently, the multiplicity pattern is

\[
(1,2,\ldots,2).
\]

For even \(q\), the ordering terminates with the single central column

\[
\tfrac q2+1 = \left\lfloor\tfrac q2\right\rfloor+1,
\]

which corresponds to the additional one-dimensional highest-frequency
eigenspace. The multiplicity pattern is therefore

\[
(1,2,\ldots,2,1).
\]

For example, for \(q=7\), the columns are ordered as

\[
1,2,7,3,6,4,5,
\]

which groups the eigenvectors as

\[
1\mid(2,7)\mid(3,6)\mid(4,5).
\]

For \(q=6\), the ordering is

\[
1,2,6,3,5,4,
\]

giving

\[
1\mid(2,6)\mid(3,5)\mid4.
\]

These groupings correspond exactly to the multiplicity vectors returned by
`basis_CT()`:

```r
basis_CT(7)$qq
# [1] 1 2 2 2

basis_CT(6)$qq
# [1] 1 2 2 1
```

Consequently, every circular Toeplitz covariance matrix admits the spectral
representation

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor q/2\rfloor+1}\lambda_i\,\mathbf V_i,
\]

where

\[
\lambda_k = \tau_0 + 2\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor(q-1)/2\rfloor}\tau_j\cos\left(\frac{2\pi kj}{q}\right)
+ \begin{cases} \tau_{q/2}(-1)^k,&q\text{ even},\\ 0,&q\text{ odd},\end{cases}
\]

and where \(\mathbf V_i\) are the projection matrices onto the subspaces spanned by the
columns of \(\mathbf H_{CT,q}\) (after permutation described above) corresponding to distinct eigenvalues (number of columns is determined by the multiplicity of eigenvalue).

The basis matrix returned by

```r
obj <- basis_CT(7)

round(obj$H, 3)
```

contains the common orthonormal eigenvectors shared by every
\(7\times7\) circular Toeplitz covariance matrix. Since \(q=7\) is odd,
the first column corresponds to the eigenvalue of mutiplicity one
whereas each subsequent pair of columns corresponds to an eigenvalue of
multiplicity two. For even dimensions, the final column similarly corresponds
to the additional simple eigenvalue associated with the highest-frequency component.

To illustrate this common eigenbasis, consider two different circular Toeplitz covariance matrices. Using the basis returned by `basis_CT(q)`, both matrices are diagonalized simultaneously.

```r
H <- basis_CT(6)$H

Omega1 <- toeplitz(c(4, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2))
Omega2 <- toeplitz(c(3, 1, 0.5, -0.2, 0.5, 1))

round(t(H) %*% Omega1 %*% H, 6)
round(t(H) %*% Omega2 %*% H, 6)
```

In both cases, the transformed matrices are diagonal, demonstrating that the
basis returned by `basis_CT(q)` diagonalizes every circular Toeplitz covariance
matrix of the given dimension. Changing the covariance parameters affects only
the eigenvalues, while the eigenvectors remain unchanged.

**Statistical interpretation:** The circular Toeplitz structure assumes that
the covariance between two variables depends only on their circular distance.
Variables separated by the same circular lag therefore have identical covariance.

From the spectral point of view, circular Toeplitz covariance matrices are
diagonalized by a discrete Fourier-type basis. This common eigenbasis makes
the spectral representation particularly attractive for statistical inference,
since the covariance structure is completely characterized by its eigenvalues.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Periodic or cyclic measurements (e.g., hours of the day, days of the week, months of the year or        repeated measurements around a circular object such as flower petals).
> - Signals observed on a circle or ring.
> - Directional and angular data.
> - Image and signal processing problems with periodic boundary conditions.


# Doubly multivariate structures

A doubly multivariate model arises when each observation is naturally
organized in two dimensions. Specifically, a \(pm\)-dimensional observation
vector is partitioned into \(p\) subvectors (or blocks), each of dimension
\(m\),

\[
\mathbf y = \left(\mathbf y_1^\top,\ldots,\mathbf y_p^\top\right)^\top,
\qquad \mathbf y_i\in\mathbb R^m.
\]

The two dimensions can have different statistical interpretations. For
example, the \(p\) blocks may correspond to subjects, experimental groups,
spatial locations, or other higher-level units, while the \(m\) variables
within each block may represent repeated measurements, response variables,
or measurement occasions.

The covariance matrix therefore has dimension \(pm\times pm\) and describes
both the covariance structure within individual blocks and the relationship
between different blocks. The basis generators provided by `TestCQS` allow
these two aspects to be specified separately through a between-block
structure and a within-block covariance structure.

In the following sections, we first consider four families of between-block structures—
block sphericity, block diagonality, block compound symmetry, and block circular
Toeplitz—and combine them with the corresponding within-block covariance structures.
This produces the doubly multivariate covariance structures implemented in
the package.

|Family|Generators|
|:------|:---------|
|Block sphericity|`basis_BS_*()`|
|Block diagonality|`basis_BD_*()`|
|Block compound symmetry|`basis_BCS_*()`|
|Block circular Toeplitz|`basis_BCT_*()`|

Each family can be combined with one of the within-block covariance structures:

- `S` – sphericity,
- `D` – diagonality,
- `CS` – compound symmetry,
- `CT` – circular Toeplitz.

Two combinations are redundant:

- `BS_S` reduces to the ordinary multivariate spherical structure `S`,
- `BD_D` reduces to the ordinary multivariate diagonal structure `D`.

Consequently, **14 distinct basis generators** are implemented  fo the
between-block/within-block construction in `TestCQS`.

The naming convention follows the pattern

```text
basis_<between-block structure>_<within-block structure>()
```

For example,

- `basis_BS_CT()` generates a block sphericity structure with circular
  Toeplitz covariance within each block,
- `basis_BCS_CS()` generates a block compound symmetry structure with
  compound symmetry within each block,
- `basis_BCT_D()` generates a block circular Toeplitz structure with
  diagonal covariance within each block.


Since these structures assume that each block of the observation vector
have the same number of observations \(m\), that is, all within-blocks
have the same dimension \(m\), the basis matrices for
doubly multivariate covariance structures are constructed by combining
a **between-block** basis with a **within-block** basis through the 
Kronecker product. Thus, every doubly multivariate basis matrix implemented in
``TestCQS`` has the unified form

\[
\boxed{
\mathbf H =\mathbf H_{\mathrm{between}} \otimes \mathbf H_{\mathrm{within}}.
}
\]

The same principle applies to the eigenvalue multiplicity vectors, that is, if
\(qq_{S}\) and \(qq_{D}\) are the eigenvalue multiplicity vectors of sphericity
and diagonality, respectively, then \(qq_{BS\_D} = qq_{S}\otimes qq_{D}\)
is the eigenvalue multiplicity vector of block sphericity structure with
diagonal blocks. This Kronecker-product construction applies to the fourteen
structures obtained by combining the four supported between-block families with the
four within-block structures, after removing the two redundant
combinations described above.

The fourteen built-in doubly multivariate basis generators therefore
follow the simple construction principle summarized below.

| Structure | Basis construction | Eigenvalue multiplicity vector |
|:----------|:-------------------|:-------------------------------|
| `BS_D` | \(\mathbf H_{S}\otimes\mathbf H_D\) | \(qq_{S}\otimes qq_{D}\) |
| `BS_CS` | \(\mathbf H_{S}\otimes\mathbf H_{CS}\) | \(qq_{S}\otimes qq_{CS}\) |
| `BS_CT` | \(\mathbf H_{S}\otimes\mathbf H_{CT}\) | \(qq_{S}\otimes qq_{CT}\) |
| `BD_S` | \(\mathbf H_{D}\otimes\mathbf H_S\) | \(qq_{D}\otimes qq_{S}\) |
| `BD_CS` | \(\mathbf H_{D}\otimes\mathbf H_{CS}\) | \(qq_{D}\otimes qq_{CS}\) |
| `BD_CT` | \(\mathbf H_{D}\otimes\mathbf H_{CT}\) | \(qq_{D}\otimes qq_{CT}\) |
| `BCS_S` | \(\mathbf H_{CS}\otimes\mathbf H_S\) | \(qq_{CS}\otimes qq_{S}\) |
| `BCS_D` | \(\mathbf H_{CS}\otimes\mathbf H_D\) | \(qq_{CS}\otimes qq_{D}\) |
| `BCS_CS` | \(\mathbf H_{CS}\otimes\mathbf H_{CS}\) | \(qq_{CS}\otimes qq_{CS}\) |
| `BCS_CT` | \(\mathbf H_{CS}\otimes\mathbf H_{CT}\) | \(qq_{CS}\otimes qq_{CT}\) |
| `BCT_S` | \(\mathbf H_{CT}\otimes\mathbf H_S\) | \(qq_{CT}\otimes qq_{S}\) |
| `BCT_D` | \(\mathbf H_{CT}\otimes\mathbf H_D\) | \(qq_{CT}\otimes qq_{D}\) |
| `BCT_CS` | \(\mathbf H_{CT}\otimes\mathbf H_{CS}\) | \(qq_{CT}\otimes qq_{CS}\) |
| `BCT_CT` | \(\mathbf H_{CT}\otimes\mathbf H_{CT}\) | \(qq_{CT}\otimes qq_{CT}\) |

The vector `qq` returned by each basis generator contains the
multiplicities of the eigenspaces represented by the columns of
\(\mathbf H\). Consequently,

```r
sum(obj$qq)
```

always equals the number of columns of `obj$H`, which is precisely the
dimension of the corresponding covariance matrix. Moreover, the dimensions
of the returned basis matrix always satisfy

```r
sum(obj$qq)
```

which equals \(pm\), the dimension of the covariance matrix.

The construction principle above covers the fourteen doubly multivariate
structures obtained by combining a between-block structure with a
within-block structure. However, they are not the only doubly multivariate
commutative quadratic structures implemented in `TestCQS`.
The package also provides two additional commutative quadratic structures
that do not arise from this direct Kronecker-product construction:

- **Uniform block structure**, and
- **Double complete symmetric structure**.

Both structures belong to the class of commutative quadratic subspaces and
therefore admit the spectral representation required by the testing
procedures implemented in `TestCQS`. However, their eigenspace
decompositions have a different form and their basis matrices are therefore
constructed separately rather than by simply taking the Kronecker product of
a between-block and a within-block basis.

Consequently, the fourteen structures listed above should be viewed as the
main family of doubly multivariate structures generated by the
between-block/within-block construction, while the uniform block and
double complete symmetry structures are additional built-in CQS models.
They are described separately in the following sections.

The final section of this vignette describes how users can construct and
use their own commutative quadratic covariance structures.



## Block sphericity family

The block sphericity family assumes that the \(pm\)-dimensional observation
vector is partitioned into \(p\) subvectors (blocks) of dimension \(m\),

\[
\mathbf y =
\left(
\mathbf y_1^\top,\ldots,\mathbf y_p^\top
\right)^\top,
\qquad
\mathbf y_i\in\mathbb R^m.
\]

The defining assumption of block sphericity is that the blocks are mutually
uncorrelated and share the same within-block covariance matrix. Thus, the
covariance matrix has the block-diagonal form

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\mathbf I_p\otimes\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
=
\left(
\begin{smallmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Lambda} & \mathbf 0_m & \cdots & \mathbf 0_m\\
\mathbf 0_m & \boldsymbol{\Lambda} & \cdots & \mathbf 0_m\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
\mathbf 0_m & \mathbf 0_m & \cdots & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}
\end{smallmatrix}
\right),
\]

where \(p\) denotes the number of blocks, \(m\) the dimension of each block,
and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is the common \(m\times m\) within-block
covariance matrix.

Thus, the covariance structure separates naturally into two components. The
between-block structure is spherical, represented by \(\mathbf I_p\), so
different blocks are mutually uncorrelated and have identical covariance
properties. The particular form of the within-block covariance matrix
\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) determines the specific member of the block
sphericity family.

In `TestCQS`, the three non-redundant members of this family are

| Structure | Within-block covariance structure | Generator |
| :-------- | :------------------------------- | :-------- |
| `BS_D`    | Diagonality                      | `basis_BS_D(p,m)` |
| `BS_CS`   | Compound symmetry                | `basis_BS_CS(p,m)` |
| `BS_CT`   | Circular Toeplitz                | `basis_BS_CT(p,m)` |

The corresponding basis matrices follow directly from the Kronecker-product
construction described above. If \(\mathbf H_{S,p}=\mathbf I_p\) denotes the
between-block basis and \(\mathbf H_{\mathrm{within},m}\) denotes the
orthogonal basis associated with the chosen within-block covariance
structure, then

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf H_{S,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{\mathrm{within},m}
=
\mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf H_{\mathrm{within},m}.
\]

Similarly, if \(\mathbf{qq}_{\mathrm{within}}\) denotes the vector of
eigenvalue multiplicities for the within-block structure, then the
multiplicity vector for the resulting block structure is

\[
\mathbf{qq}
=
\mathbf{1}_p\otimes\mathbf{qq}_{\mathrm{within}},
\]

where \(\mathbf 1_p\) denotes the \(p\)-dimensional vector of ones.

Equivalently, each eigenvalue of the within-block covariance matrix occurs
once in every block and therefore has its within-block multiplicity multiplied
by \(p\).

The following subsections describe the three members of the block sphericity
family in detail.

### Block sphericity with diagonal within-block structure (BS_D)

The `BS_D` structure is obtained when the common within-block covariance
matrix is diagonal,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
=
\operatorname{diag}
(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m).
\]

Consequently,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\mathbf I_p\otimes
\operatorname{diag}
(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m).
\]

The variables within each block are therefore mutually uncorrelated, while
each variable may have its own variance. Since the same diagonal covariance
matrix is repeated across all \(p\) blocks, variables occupying the same
position in different blocks have the same variance.

From the spectral point of view,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{m}
\lambda_i
\left(
\mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf E_{ii}
\right),
\]

where \(\mathbf E_{ii}\) is the projection matrix onto the \(i\)-th coordinate
axis of \(\mathbb R^m\).

Thus, each within-block eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) occurs in all \(p\) blocks.
Assuming the \(m\) diagonal elements are distinct, the covariance matrix has
\(m\) distinct eigenvalues, each with multiplicity \(p\).

For example,

```r
obj <- basis_BS_D(p = 3, m = 4)

obj$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 3 3 3 3
```

indicating that the covariance matrix has four distinct eigenvalues, each
with multiplicity three.

The corresponding basis matrix is

\[
\mathbf H = \mathbf H_{S,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{D,m} = \mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf I_m = \mathbf I_{pm},
\]

with its columns ordered according to the repeated within-block eigenvalues.
Each group of \(p\) columns corresponds to one within-block eigenvalue.

**Statistical interpretation:** This `BS_D` structure assumes that

- all blocks are statistically identical,
- different blocks are mutually uncorrelated,
- variables within each block are mutually uncorrelated,
- the variance associated with a given within-block variable is the same across all blocks.

Thus, variables occupying the same position within different blocks have
the same variance, while different within-block variables may have
different variances.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Repeated measurements on several independent experimental units when each
    measurement variable has its own variance.
> - Multisite experiments where sites are independent but identical variables
    are measured at each site.
> - Balanced multilevel studies with independent groups and heterogeneous
    within-group variances.

### Block sphericity with compound symmetry within-block structure (BS_CS)

The BS_CS structure is obtained when the common within-block covariance
matrix follows compound symmetry,

\[
\mathbf\Lambda = \sigma^2(1-\rho)\mathbf I_m + \sigma^2\rho\mathbf J_m = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}
\sigma^2 & \sigma^2\rho & \cdots & \sigma^2\rho \\
\sigma^2\rho & \sigma^2 & \cdots & \sigma^2\rho \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\sigma^2\rho & \sigma^2\rho & \cdots & \sigma^2
\end{smallmatrix}\right).
\]

Consequently,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\sigma^2(1-\rho)(\mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf I_m) + \sigma^2\rho(\mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf J_m).
\]

Thus, different blocks are mutually uncorrelated and have the same compound
symmetry covariance structure. Within each block, all variables have the same
variance and every pair of distinct variables has the same covariance.

Using the spectral decomposition of the compound symmetry structure,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \lambda_1\mathbf P_{1_m}
+ \lambda_2\mathbf Q_{1_m},
\]

where

\[
\lambda_1=\sigma^2(1+(m-1)\rho), \qquad \lambda_2=\sigma^2(1-\rho).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \lambda_1\left(\mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf P_{1_m}\right)
+ \lambda_2\left(\mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf Q_{1_m}\right).
\]

The first eigenvalue has multiplicity \(p\), since the mean direction occurs
once in every block. The second eigenvalue has multiplicity \(p(m−1)\),
corresponding to the orthogonal contrast subspace within each block.

Thus,

\[
\mathbf{qq}_{BS\_CS} = (p, p(m-1)).
\]

For example,

```r
obj <- basis_BS_CS(p = 3, m = 4)

obj$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 3 9
```

The first entry corresponds to the eigenspace generated by the constant direction within each block, while the second corresponds to the orthogonal contrast subspace of dimension \(m−1\), repeated across all \(p\) blocks.

The corresponding basis matrix is

\[
\mathbf H=\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}(\mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf 1_m):
\mathbf I_p\otimes\widetilde{\mathbf Q}
\right),
\]

where \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\) is an \(m\times m-1\) matrix representing any orthonormal basis of the subspace orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_m\).

Consequently, the first \(p\) columns of the resulting basis correspond to
the common mean direction within each block, while the remaining
\(p(m−1)\) columns span the within-block contrast spaces.

**Statistical interpretation:** The `BS_CS` structure assumes that

- all blocks have identical compound symmetry covariance matrices,
- different blocks are mutually uncorrelated,
- variables within a block have a common variance,
- every pair of variables within a block has the same covariance.

Consequently, variables measured within the same block are
exchangeable—the covariance depends only on whether two observations
coincide or not.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Repeated measurements in which all observations within a subject are
    equally correlated.
> - Clustered or longitudinal data under the exchangeability assumption.
> - Balanced multilevel experiments where measurements within each group
    have a common correlation.
> - Educational or psychological studies in which responses within an
    individual are assumed to be equally correlated.


### Block sphericity with circular Toeplitz within-block structure (BS_CT)

The `BS_CT` structure is obtained when the common within-block covariance
matrix follows a circular Toeplitz structure,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \operatorname{Toep}(\tau_0,\tau_1,\tau_2,\tau_{\lfloor q/2\rfloor},
\tau_{\lfloor q/2\rfloor-1},\ldots,\tau_2,\tau_1).
\]

Consequently,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\mathbf I_p
\otimes
\operatorname{Toep}(\tau_0,\tau_1,\tau_2,\tau_{\lfloor q/2\rfloor},
\tau_{\lfloor q/2\rfloor-1},\ldots,\tau_2,\tau_1).
\]

Different blocks are mutually uncorrelated and have the same circular
Toeplitz covariance structure. Within each block, the covariance between two
variables depends only on their circular distance.

The spectral decomposition of the within-block circular Toeplitz matrix
provides a common orthogonal basis \(\mathbf H_{CT,m}\). Hence,

\[
\mathbf H = \mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf H_{CT,m}.
\]

The multiplicities of the resulting eigenvalues are obtained by multiplying
the within-block multiplicities by \(p\). Thus, for odd \(m\),

\[
\mathbf{qq}_{BS\_CT} = (p, 2p, \ldots, 2p),
\]

whereas for even \(m\),

\[
\mathbf{qq}_{BS\_CT} = (p, 2p, \ldots, 2p, p).
\]


For example,

```r
obj <- basis_BS_CT(p = 3, m = 7)

obj$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 3 6 6 6
```

while for an even within-block dimension,

```r
basis_BS_CT(p = 3, m = 6)$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 3 6 6 3
```

The basis matrix is

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf H_{CT,m},
\]

where \(\mathbf H_{CT,m}\) is the circular Toeplitz basis described in the
Circular Toeplitz subsection above. Thus, the same Fourier-type directions
are used within every block.

**Statistical interpretation:** The `BS_CT` structure assumes that

- all \(m\)-dimensional blocks share the same circular Toeplitz covariance
  structure,
- different blocks are mutually uncorrelated,
- within each block, the covariance between two variables depends only on
  their circular distance.

Consequently, the covariance structure within each block is invariant under
cyclic permutations of the variables.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Periodic repeated measurements collected independently on several 
    experimental units.
> - Multichannel signals recorded independently on several sensors arranged
    on a circle or ring.
> - Directional or angular measurements obtained from independent subjects.
> - Image and signal processing problems with periodic boundary conditions
    within independent experimental units.



## Block diagonality family

The block diagonality family assumes that the \(pm\)-dimensional observation
vector is partitioned into \(p\) subvectors (blocks) of dimension \(m\),

\[
\mathbf y =
\left(
\mathbf y_1^\top,\ldots,\mathbf y_p^\top
\right)^\top,
\qquad
\mathbf y_i\in\mathbb R^m.
\]

The defining feature of block diagonality is that the covariance matrix is
block diagonal. In contrast to block sphericity, the covariance structure
may differ from one block to another. Thus, if the \(pm\)-dimensional
observation vector is partitioned into \(p\) subvectors of dimension \(m\),
the covariance matrix has the general form

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\left(
\begin{smallmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1 & \mathbf 0_m & \cdots & \mathbf 0_m\\
\mathbf 0_m & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf 0_m\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
\mathbf 0_m & \mathbf 0_m & \cdots & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_p
\end{smallmatrix}
\right),
\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\) is the \(m\times m\) covariance matrix
associated with the \(i\)-th block.

Thus, different blocks are mutually uncorrelated, while each block may have
its own covariance structure. The within-block structures considered in
`TestCQS` determine the particular form of the matrices
\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_p\).

In the spectral construction used by `TestCQS`, each block is represented by
its own eigenvalues and eigenspaces. Consequently, unlike block sphericity,
the eigenvalues need not be repeated across blocks. The corresponding basis
matrix is obtained by combining the eigenvector bases of the individual
blocks,

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf H_{D,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{\mathrm{within}} = \mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf H_{\mathrm{within}}.
\]

The eigenvalue multiplicities are determined by the multiplicities of the
within-block eigenvalues. In particular, each within-block eigenspace is
replicated across the \(p\) blocks. Unlike block sphericity, however, the
corresponding eigenvalues need not be equal across blocks.

The three non-redundant members of the block diagonality family are

| Structure | Within-block covariance structure | Generator |
| :-------- | :------------------------------- | :-------- |
| `BD_S`    | Sphericity                       | `basis_BD_S(p,m)` |
| `BD_CS`   | Compound symmetry                | `basis_BD_CS(p,m)` |
| `BD_CT`   | Circular Toeplitz                | `basis_BD_CT(p,m)` |

The combination `BD_D` is not listed because it reduces to the ordinary
multivariate diagonal structure `D`.

The following subsections describe the three members of the block
diagonality family in detail.

### Block diagonality with sphericity within-block structure (BD_S)

The `BD_S` structure is obtained when each block has a spherical covariance
matrix, while the covariance matrices of different blocks are allowed to
differ. Thus,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\operatorname{diag}
\left(
\lambda_1\mathbf I_m,
\lambda_2\mathbf I_m,
\ldots,
\lambda_p\mathbf I_m
\right)
=
\left(\begin{smallmatrix}
\lambda_1\mathbf I_m & \mathbf 0_m & \cdots & \mathbf 0_m\\
\mathbf 0_m & \lambda_2\mathbf I_m & \cdots & \mathbf 0_m\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
\mathbf 0_m & \mathbf 0_m & \cdots & \lambda_p\mathbf I_m
\end{smallmatrix}\right).
\]

Here \(\lambda_i\) represents the common variance of the \(m\) variables
within the \(i\)-th block. Thus, variables within a given block are
mutually uncorrelated and have the same variance, while the common variance
may differ between blocks.

From the spectral point of view, the covariance matrix can be written as

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{p}
\lambda_i
\left(
\mathbf E_{ii}\otimes\mathbf I_m
\right).
\]

Consequently, assuming that the \(p\) block-specific variances are distinct,
the covariance matrix has \(p\) distinct eigenvalues, each with multiplicity
\(m\). The multiplicity \(m\) reflects the fact that the same variance
\(\lambda_i\) applies to all \(m\) variables within the \(i\)-th block.

For example,

```r
obj <- basis_BD_S(p = 3, m = 4)

obj$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 4 4 4
```

indicating that the covariance matrix has three distinct eigenvalues, each
with multiplicity four.

The corresponding basis matrix is

\[
\mathbf H = \mathbf H_{D,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{S,m} = \mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf I_m = \mathbf I_{pm}.
\]

Although the resulting basis matrix is the identity, its columns are
ordered according to the block-specific eigenvalues. Thus, the first
\(m\) columns correspond to the first block and its eigenvalue
\(\lambda_i\), the next\(m\) columns to the second block and \(\lambda_2\), and so on.

**Statistical interpretation:** The `BD_S` structure assumes that

- different blocks are mutually uncorrelated,
- each block has its own variance,
- variables within each block are uncorrelated,
- all variables within a block have the same variance.

Thus, every block is spherical, although the variance may differ from one
block to another.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Independent groups of variables measured on different scales, where
    each group is assumed to be isotropic.
> - Multisensor experiments in which each sensor produces independent
    isotropic measurement noise with a sensor-specific variance.
> - Block-structured multivariate data in which the overall variability
    differs across blocks, while variables within each block are exchangeable
    only through a common variance.


### Block diagonality with compound symmetry within-block structure (BD_CS)

The `BD_CS` structure is obtained when each block has a compound symmetry
covariance structure, while the covariance matrices of different blocks are
allowed to differ. Thus,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\operatorname{diag}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1,
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2,
\ldots,
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_p
\right) = 
\left(
\begin{smallmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1 & \mathbf 0_m & \cdots & \mathbf 0_m\\
\mathbf 0_m & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf 0_m\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
\mathbf 0_m & \mathbf 0_m & \cdots & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_p
\end{smallmatrix}
\right),
\]

where the covariance matrix of the \(i\)-th block is

\[
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i
=
\sigma_i^2(1-\rho_i)\mathbf I_m
+
\sigma_i^2\rho_i\mathbf J_m,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,p.
\]

Here, \(\sigma_i^2\) represents the common variance of the variables
within the \(i\)-th block, while \(\rho_i\) represents their common
pairwise correlation. Thus, variables within a block are exchangeable,
whereas the covariance parameters may differ between blocks.

Using the spectral representation of compound symmetry,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{p}
\left[
\lambda_{i1}
\left(
\mathbf E_{ii}\otimes\mathbf P_{1_m}
\right)
+
\lambda_{i2}
\left(
\mathbf E_{ii}\otimes\mathbf Q_{1_m}
\right)
\right],
\]

where

\[
\lambda_{i1}
=
\sigma_i^2\left(1+(m-1)\rho_i\right),
\qquad
\lambda_{i2}
=
\sigma_i^2(1-\rho_i).
\]

Thus, each block contributes two eigenspaces:

- the one-dimensional mean direction within the block, corresponding to
  \(\lambda_{i,1}\);
- the \((m-1)\)-dimensional contrast subspace orthogonal to the mean
  direction, corresponding to \(\lambda_{i,2}\).

Assuming that the resulting eigenvalues are distinct across blocks, the
covariance matrix has \(2p\) distinct eigenvalues. Their multiplicities are

\[
(\underbrace{1,m-1}_{\text{Block 1}},
\underbrace{1,m-1}_{\text{Block 2}},
\ldots,
\underbrace{1,m-1}_{\text{Block }p}).
\]

For example,

```r
obj <- basis_BD_CS(p = 3, m = 4)

obj$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 1 3 1 3 1 3
```

showing that each of the three blocks contributes one one-dimensional
eigenspace associated with the normalized constant vector and one
three-dimensional contrast eigenspace.

The corresponding basis matrix is

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf H_{D,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{CS,m}= \mathbf I_{p}\otimes\mathbf H_{CS,m},
\]

where

\[
\mathbf H_{CS,m} = \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\mathbf1_m:\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\right)
\]

is the compound symmetry basis described in the Compound symmetry
subsection, and \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\) is \(m\times m-1\) matrix representing an orthonormal basis of the
subspace orthogonal to \(\mathbf1_m\).

**Statistical interpretation:** The `BD_CS` structure assumes that

- different blocks are mutually uncorrelated,
- each block has its own variance,
- each block has its own common correlation,
- variables within the same block are exchangeable.

Unlike `BS_CS`, where all blocks share a common compound symmetry
covariance matrix, `BD_CS` allows both the variance and the correlation to
vary from block to block.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Longitudinal studies where repeated measurements are grouped into
    independent outcomes, each exhibiting exchangeable dependence with its
    own variability.
> - Multivariate experiments in which different measurement modalities are
    independent, but repeated observations within each modality have compound symmetry.
> - Educational or psychological studies involving several independent
    subscales, each characterized by its own variance and common within-subscale correlation.


### Block diagonality with circular Toeplitz within-block structure (BD_CT)

The `BD_CT` structure is obtained when each block has a circular Toeplitz
covariance structure, while the covariance matrices of different blocks are
allowed to differ. Thus,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\operatorname{diag}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1,
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2,
\ldots,
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_p
\right) = 
\left(
\begin{smallmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1 & \mathbf 0_m & \cdots & \mathbf 0_m\\
\mathbf 0_m & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf 0_m\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
\mathbf 0_m & \mathbf 0_m & \cdots & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_p
\end{smallmatrix}
\right),
\]

where each \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\) is an \(m\times m\) circular Toeplitz
covariance matrix

\[
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i
=
\operatorname{Toep}
\left(
\tau_{i,0},
\tau_{i,1},
\ldots,
\tau_{i,\lfloor m/2\rfloor},
\ldots,
\tau_{i,1}
\right).
\]

Thus, different blocks are mutually uncorrelated, while the covariance
within each block follows a circular Toeplitz structure. The circular
Toeplitz parameters may differ between blocks.

From the spectral point of view, each block is diagonalized by the same
circular Toeplitz basis \(\mathbf H_{CT,m}\). Consequently,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i
=
\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor+1}
\lambda_{i,j}\mathbf V_j,
\]

where the projection matrices \(\mathbf V_j\) are those appearing in the
spectral decomposition of the ordinary circular Toeplitz covariance
structure (see the *Circular Toeplitz* section).

The complete covariance matrix can therefore be written as

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{p}
\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor+1}
\lambda_{i,j}
\left(
\mathbf E_{ii}\otimes\mathbf V_j
\right).
\]

This representation shows that each block contributes its own set of
circular Toeplitz eigenvalues, while the corresponding within-block
eigenspaces have the same Fourier-type basis across all blocks.

Consequently, each block contributes
\(\lfloor m/2\rfloor+1\) distinct eigenvalues, having the same
multiplicity pattern as the ordinary circular Toeplitz structure.
Therefore,

- if \(m\) is odd, the multiplicities are

\[
(\underbrace{1,2,\ldots,2}_{\text{Block 1}},
\underbrace{1,2,\ldots,2}_{\text{Block 2}},
\ldots,
\underbrace{1,2,\ldots,2}_{\text{Block }p}),
\]

- if \(m\) is even, the multiplicities are

\[
(\underbrace{1,2,\ldots,2,1}_{\text{Block 1}},
\underbrace{1,2,\ldots,2,1}_{\text{Block 2}},
\ldots,
\underbrace{1,2,\ldots,2,1}_{\text{Block }p}).
\]

This reflects the fact that each block possesses its own circular
Toeplitz covariance structure, while different blocks are mutually
uncorrelated.

For example, for an odd block dimension \(m=7\),

```r
obj <- basis_BD_CT(p = 3, m = 7)

obj$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 1 2 2 2 1 2 2 2 1 2 2 2
```

whereas for even \(m=6\),

```r
basis_BD_CT(p = 3, m = 6)$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 1 2 2 1 1 2 2 1 1 2 2 1
```

Each block contributes one one-dimensional eigenspace corresponding to the
normalized constant vector, several two-dimensional eigenspaces
corresponding to the remaining circular frequencies, and, for even values
of \(m\), one additional one-dimensional highest-frequency eigenspace.

The corresponding basis matrix is

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf H_{D,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{CT,m} = \mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf H_{CT,m}.
\]

The basis \(\mathbf H_{CT,m}\) is the common circular Toeplitz eigenbasis
described in the *Circular Toeplitz* subsection. Consequently, the same
within-block eigenvectors are used for every block, although the associated
eigenvalues may differ from block to block.

The columns of the resulting basis matrix are ordered block by block.
Within each block, the columns follow the ordering of \(\mathbf H_{CT,m}\),
so that columns corresponding to the same
within-block eigenvalue are consecutive.

For example, when p=3 and m=7, the multiplicity structure is

\[(1,2,2,2)\,|\,(1,2,2,2)\,∣\,(1,2,2,2,)\]

where each group corresponds to one block.

**Statistical interpretation:** The `BD_CT` structure assumes that

- different blocks are mutually uncorrelated,
- each block has its own circular Toeplitz covariance matrix,
- within each block, covariance depends only on the circular distance
  between variables,
- the circular dependence pattern may differ from one block to another.

Unlike `BS_CT`, where all blocks share a common circular Toeplitz
covariance structure, `BD_CT` allows every block to have its own set of
circular Toeplitz parameters.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Several independent periodic signals, each exhibiting its own cyclic
    dependence structure.
> - Multichannel recordings in which each channel consists of circularly
    ordered measurements with channel-specific covariance parameters.
> - Environmental or meteorological measurements collected over periodic
    cycles for several independent locations.
> - Image or signal processing problems involving independent periodic
    components with different covariance characteristics.


## Block compound symmetry family

The block compound symmetry family assumes that the \(pm\)-dimensional observation
vector is partitioned into \(p\) subvectors (blocks) of dimension \(m\),

\[
\mathbf y =
\left(
\mathbf y_1^\top,\ldots,\mathbf y_p^\top
\right)^\top,
\qquad
\mathbf y_i\in\mathbb R^m.
\]

The defining feature of block compound symmetry is
that the covariance structure between the blocks follows compound symmetry,
while a separate covariance structure is specified within each block. The covariance matrix has the general form

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
= \mathbf I_p\otimes(\boldsymbol\Gamma_0-\boldsymbol\Gamma_1) + \mathbf J_p\otimes\boldsymbol\Gamma_1 = 
\left(
\begin{smallmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0 & \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 & \cdots & \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1\\
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 & \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0 & \cdots & \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 & \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 & \cdots & \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0
\end{smallmatrix}
\right),
\]

where \(m \times m\) diagonal blocks \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0\) represent the covariance
matrix of the \(m\) response variables within each of the \(p\) subvectors, and \(m \times m\) off-diagonal
blocks \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1\) represent the covariance matrix of the \(m\) response
variables between any two subvectors.

Thus, the subvectors are exchangeable, which means that the covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol\Omega\)
remains unchanged under any permutation of the \(p\) subvectors.

Equivalently, using the spectral representation of the compound symmetry
structure between the blocks,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \mathbf P_{1_p}\otimes\boldsymbol\Lambda_1 + \mathbf Q_{1_p}\otimes\boldsymbol\Lambda_2,
\]

where

\[
\boldsymbol\Lambda_1=\boldsymbol\Gamma_0 + (p-1)\boldsymbol\Gamma_1,\qquad \boldsymbol\Lambda_2=\boldsymbol\Gamma_0-\boldsymbol\Gamma_1.
\]

Here, \(\boldsymbol\Lambda_1\) is the within-block covariance matrix
associated with the between-block mean direction spanned by
\(\mathbf 1_p\), whereas \(\boldsymbol\Lambda_2\) is the within-block
covariance matrix associated with the \((p-1)\)-dimensional subspace
orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_p\).

In the spectral construction used by `TestCQS`, the basis matrix is obtained
by combining the eigenvector basis for the between-block compound symmetry
structure with the corresponding within-block basis. Thus,

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf H_{CS,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{\mathrm{within}} = 
\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\mathbf 1_p\otimes\mathbf H_{\mathrm{within}} :
\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\otimes\mathbf H_{\mathrm{within}}\right),
\]

where \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\) is a \(p\times p-1\) matrix representing any orthonormal
basis of the subspace orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_p\).
Consequently, the between-block structure has two eigenspaces:

- the one-dimensional subspace spanned by the constant vector
  \(\mathbf 1_p\), corresponding to the within-block covariance matrix
  \(\boldsymbol\Lambda_1\);
- the \((p-1)\)-dimensional subspace orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_p\),
  corresponding to the within-block covariance matrix
  \(\boldsymbol\Lambda_2\).

The within-block covariance structure can independently be chosen as
sphericity, diagonality, compound symmetry, or circular Toeplitz. This gives
the four structures

| Structure | Within-block covariance structure | Generator |
| :-------- | :------------------------------- | :-------- |
| `BCS_S`    | Sphericity                       | `basis_BCS_S(p,m)` |
| `BCS_D`    | Diagonality                       | `basis_BCS_D(p,m)` |
| `BCS_CS`   | Compound symmetry                | `basis_BCS_CS(p,m)` |
| `BCS_CT`   | Circular Toeplitz                | `basis_BCS_CT(p,m)` |

The following subsections describe the four members of the block
compound symmetry family in detail.


### Block compound symmetry with spherical within-block structure (BCS_S)

The `BCS_S` structure is obtained when the within-block covariance
matrices are spherical. Thus, the general block compound symmetry
representation is specialized by taking

\[
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0=\sigma^2\mathbf I_m,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1=\sigma^2\rho\mathbf I_m.
\]

Consequently, the covariance matrix has the form

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\mathbf I_p\otimes
\left[(\sigma^2(1-\rho)\mathbf I_m\right]
+
\mathbf J_p\otimes
\left(\sigma^2\rho\mathbf I_m\right).
\]

Thus, all variables within a block have the same variance, while the
covariance between corresponding variables in two distinct blocks is the
same. Since the within-block covariance matrices are proportional to the
identity, variables corresponding to different positions within a block
are uncorrelated.

Using the spectral representation of compound symmetry, the covariance
matrix can be written as

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\lambda_1
\left(\mathbf P_{1_p}\otimes\mathbf I_m\right)
+
\lambda_2
\left(\mathbf Q_{1_p}\otimes\mathbf I_m\right),
\]

where

\[
\lambda_1
=
\sigma^2(1+(p-1)\rho),
\qquad
\lambda_2
=
\sigma^2(1-\rho).
\]

The first eigenvalue corresponds to the common direction across the
\(p\) blocks, whereas the second corresponds to contrasts between blocks.
Because the within-block covariance is spherical, both between-block
eigenspaces are repeated identically over all \(m\) within-block
directions.

Consequently, the covariance matrix has two distinct eigenvalues, with
multiplicities

\[
m
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
m(p-1),
\]

respectively.

For example,

```r
obj <- basis_BCS_S(p = 3, m = 4)

obj$qq
```

returns

```r
[1] 4 8
```

indicating that the first eigenvalue has multiplicity \(m=4\), while the
second has multiplicity \(m(p−1) = 8\).

The corresponding basis matrix is obtained as the Kronecker product of
the compound symmetry basis for the p blocks and the identity basis
for the \(m\)-dimensional within-block space:

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf H_{CS,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{S,m} = \mathbf H_{CS,p}\otimes\mathbf I_m.
\]

In particular,

\[
\mathbf H = \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\mathbf 1_p\otimes\mathbf I_m :
\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\otimes\mathbf I_m\right),
\]

where \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\) is any orthonormal basis of the
\((p−1)\)-dimensional subspace orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_p\).

The first \(m\) columns therefore span the eigenspace associated with
\(\lambda_1\). They correspond to the common direction across blocks,
with each of the m within-block coordinates contributing one
orthogonal direction. The remaining \(m(p−1)\) columns span the eigenspace
associated with \(\lambda_2\), representing contrasts between blocks
for each within-block coordinate.

The multiplicity vector returned by the package therefore agrees with
the Kronecker-product construction,

\[
\mathbf{qq}_{BCS\_S} = \mathbf{qq}_{CS,p}\otimes \mathbf{qq}_{S,m} = (1,p-1)\otimes (m) = (m, m(p-1)).
\]

**Statistical interpretation:** The `BCS_S` structure assumes that

- the \(p\) blocks are exchangeable;
- the covariance structure between blocks follows compound symmetry;
- all variables within a block have the same variance;
- variables occupying different positions within a block are uncorrelated;
- the within-block covariance structure is identical for all blocks.

Thus, the model distinguishes only between variation that is common across
the blocks and variation that represents contrasts between blocks. Within
each of these two between-block components, all \(m\) within-block
directions have the same variance.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Repeated multivariate measurements in which different occasions are
    equally correlated, while variables recorded at each occasion are
    independent with common variance.
> - Clustered experiments where exchangeability is assumed between groups,
    but measurements within each group are isotropic.
> - Balanced experiments with exchangeable experimental units and
    spherical within-unit covariance.
> - Longitudinal studies in which dependence is driven primarily by the
    correlation between measurement occasions rather than by the variables
    observed within each occasion.


### Block compound symmetry with diagonal within-block structure (BCS_D)

The `BCS_D` structure is obtained when the within-block covariance
matrices are diagonal. Thus, in the general block compound symmetry
representation, we take

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \left(\sigma^2(1-\rho)\mathbf I_p + \sigma^2\rho\mathbf J_p\right)
\otimes\operatorname{diag}(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_m),
\]

or, equivalently,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i1}\left(\mathbf P_{1_p}\otimes\mathbf E_{ii}\right)
+ \sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i2}\left(\mathbf Q_{1_p}\otimes\mathbf E_{ii}\right),
\]

where

\[
\lambda_{i1} = \delta_i\sigma^2(1+(p-1)\rho),\qquad \lambda_{i2} = \delta_i\sigma^2(1-\rho).
\]

Consequently, the covariance matrix has \(2m\) distinct eigenvalues.
Each within-block coordinate contributes one eigenvalue associated with
the common block direction and one associated with the orthogonal block
contrasts.

This reflects the fact that every within-block variable has its own
variance, while the dependence between blocks follows compound symmetry.

For example,

```r
obj <- basis_BCS_D(p = 3, m = 4)

obj$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 1 1 1 1 2 2 2 2
```

showing that the first four eigenspaces are one-dimensional and
correspond to the common block direction, whereas the remaining four
eigenspaces have multiplicity two and correspond to contrasts between
blocks.

The corresponding basis matrix is

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf H_{CS,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{D,m} = \mathbf H_{CS,p}\otimes\mathbf I_m.
\]

More explicitly,

\[
\mathbf H = \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\mathbf 1_p\otimes\mathbf I_m :
\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\otimes\mathbf I_m\right),
\]

where \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\) is any orthonormal basis of the
\((p−1)\)-dimensional subspace orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_p\).

The first \(m\) columns correspond to the common between-block directions,
one for each within-block variable. Each of these eigenspaces is
one-dimensional. The remaining \(m(p−1)\) columns correspond to
between-block contrasts, with \(p−1\) orthogonal directions for each
within-block variable.

The multiplicity vector returned by the package is therefore consistent
with the Kronecker-product construction,

\[
\mathbf{qq}_{BCS\_D} = \mathbf{qq}_{CS,p}\otimes \mathbf{qq}_{D,m} = (1,p-1)\otimes (1,\ldots,1),
\]

that is

\[
\mathbf{qq}_{BCS\_D} = (\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{m \text{ times}},
\underbrace{p-1,\ldots,p-1}_{m\text{ times}}).
\]


**Statistical interpretation:** The `BCS_D` structure assumes that

- the p blocks are exchangeable;
- the covariance structure between blocks follows compound symmetry;
- variables occupying different positions within a block are uncorrelated;
- the variance of each within-block variable may differ from that of the other within-block variables;
- the covariance between corresponding variables in different blocks may also depend on the within-block variable.

Thus, the model allows different within-block variables to have different
variability and different levels of between-block dependence, while
retaining exchangeability of the blocks.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Repeated multivariate measurements in which different occasions are
    equally correlated, while individual variables exhibit different variability.
> - Longitudinal studies with exchangeable dependence between measurement
    occasions and heterogeneous measurement variances.
> - Balanced clustered designs with independent within-block variables
    but exchangeable dependence between blocks.
> - Multi-endpoint experiments where endpoints are independent within each
    occasion but repeated observations remain equally correlated.


### Block compound symmetry with compound symmetry within-block structure (BCS_CS)

The `BCS_CS` structure is obtained when the within-block covariance
matrices also follow compound symmetry. Thus, in the general block
compound symmetry representation,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0
=
\sigma_0^2(1-\rho_0)\mathbf I_m
+
\sigma_0^2\rho_0\mathbf J_m, \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1
=
\sigma_1^2(1-\rho_1)\mathbf I_m
+
\sigma_1^2\rho_1\mathbf J_m.
\]

The covariance matrix therefore has the form

\[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\Omega} &= (\sigma_0^2(1-\rho_0)-\sigma_1^2(1-\rho_1))\mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf I_m
+ (\sigma_0^2\rho_0-\sigma_1^2\rho_1)\mathbf I_p\otimes\mathbf J_m + \\
&\quad + \sigma_1^2(1-\rho_1)\mathbf J_p\otimes\mathbf I_m
+ \sigma_1^2\rho_1\mathbf J_p\otimes\mathbf J_m.
\end{aligned}
\]

Equivalently, this can be written in the spectral form,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \lambda_{11}(\mathbf P_{1,p}\otimes\mathbf P_{1,m})
+ \lambda_{12}(\mathbf P_{1,p}\otimes\mathbf Q_{1,m})
+ \lambda_{21}(\mathbf Q_{1,p}\otimes\mathbf P_{1,m})
+ \lambda_{22}(\mathbf Q_{1,p}\otimes\mathbf Q_{1,m}),
\]

where

\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_{11} &= \sigma^2_0(1+(m-1)\rho_0)+(p-1)\sigma^2_1(1+(m-1)\rho_1), \\
\lambda_{12} &= \sigma^2_0(1-\rho_0)+(p-1)\sigma^2_1(1-\rho_1), \\
\lambda_{21} &= \sigma^2_0(1+(m-1)\rho_0)-\sigma^2_1(1+(m-1)\rho_1),\\
\lambda_{22} &= \sigma^2_0(1-\rho_0)-\sigma^2_1(1-\rho_1).
\end{aligned}
\]



Consequently, the covariance matrix has four distinct eigenspaces whose
multiplicities are obtained by multiplying the multiplicities of the
between-block and within-block compound symmetry structures,

\[
\bigl(1,\;m-1,\;p-1,\;(p-1)(m-1)\bigr).
\]

For example,

```r
obj <- basis_BCS_CS(p = 3, m = 4)

obj$qq
```

returns

```
[1] 1 3 2 6
```

indicating that the four eigenspaces have dimensions

\[
1,\quad m-1=3,\quad p-1=2,\quad (p-1)(m-1)=6.
\]

The four eigenspaces have a natural interpretation. The first corresponds
to the direction that is constant both across blocks and within each
block. The second represents within-block contrasts that are common
across blocks. The third represents contrasts between blocks in the
within-block mean direction. Finally, the fourth combines contrasts
between blocks with within-block contrasts.

The corresponding basis matrix is

\[
\mathbf H = \mathbf H_{CS,p} \otimes \mathbf H_{CS,m} = \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\mathbf 1_p :
\widetilde{\mathbf Q}_p\right)\otimes \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\mathbf 1_m :
\widetilde{\mathbf Q}_m\right),
\]

where \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}_p\) and \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}_m\) are
orthonormal bases of the subspaces orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_p\) and \(\mathbf 1_m\), respectively.

The Kronecker-product construction gives

\[
\mathbf{qq}_{BCS\_CS} = \mathbf{qq}_{CS,p}\otimes \mathbf{qq}_{CS,m} = (1,p-1)\otimes (1,m-1),
\]

which yields

\[
(1, m-1, p-1, (p-1)(m-1)).
\]


**Statistical interpretation:** The `BCS_CS` structure assumes that

- the p blocks are exchangeable;
- the covariance structure between blocks follows compound symmetry;
- variables within each block have a common variance;
- every pair of distinct variables within a block has the same covariance;
- the within-block compound symmetry structure is identical across blocks.

Thus, both dimensions of the doubly multivariate observation are treated
symmetrically. The model distinguishes between common and contrast
directions at the block level and, independently, between common and
contrast directions within each block.

From the spectral point of view, this produces four natural components:
the overall common direction, within-block contrasts shared across
blocks, between-block contrasts in the common within-block direction,
and simultaneous between-block and within-block contrasts.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Balanced longitudinal studies in which repeated observations are
    equally correlated over time and several outcomes are themselves exchangeable.
> - Clustered multivariate experiments where clusters are exchangeable and
    measurements within each cluster are also exchangeable.
> - Balanced clustered designs in which both the blocks and the variables
    within each block are treated as exchangeable.
> - Educational or psychological studies with several exchangeable groups
    of exchangeable measurements.
> - Repeated multivariate measurements where both the dependence between
    occasions and the dependence among variables within each occasion are
    adequately described by compound symmetry.

### Block compound symmetry with circular Toeplitz within-block structure (BCS_CT)

The `BCS_CT` structure is obtained when the within-block covariance
matrices follow the circular Toeplitz (CT) structure. Thus, in the general
block compound symmetry representation,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\mathbf I_p\otimes(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0-\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1)
+
\mathbf J_p\otimes\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1,
\]

where both \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1\) are
\(m\times m\) circular Toeplitz matrices. More precisely,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i
=
\operatorname{Toep}
(\tau_{i0},\tau_{i1},\ldots,\tau_{i,\lfloor m/2\rfloor},
\ldots,\tau_{i1}), \qquad i=0,1,
\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0\) describes the covariance structure within each block, whereas \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1\) describes the covariance structure between any two distinct blocks.

Thus, the blocks are exchangeable, as in the general block compound
symmetry family, while the covariance within and between blocks depends
on the circular distance between the corresponding within-block
variables.

Using the spectral representation of the block compound symmetry
structure,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\mathbf P_{1_p}\otimes\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1
+
\mathbf Q_{1_p}\otimes\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2,
\]

where

\[
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1
=
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0+(p-1)\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2
=
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0-\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1.
\]

Since linear combinations of circular Toeplitz matrices are again
circular Toeplitz, both \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1\) and
\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2\) are circular Toeplitz matrices of dimension
\(m\). Consequently, they are simultaneously diagonalized by the common
circular Toeplitz basis \(\mathbf H_{CT,m}\).

The resulting basis matrix is therefore the Kronecker product

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf H_{CS,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{CT,m}.
\]

Thus, the first factor describes the two eigenspaces induced by compound
symmetry between the blocks, while the second factor describes the
eigenspaces induced by the circular Toeplitz structure within the blocks.

The block compound symmetry structure contributes the two between-block
eigenspaces

- the one-dimensional space spanned by \(\mathbf 1_p\), corresponding to
  the common direction across blocks;
- the \((p-1)\)-dimensional space orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_p\),
  corresponding to contrasts between blocks.

The circular Toeplitz structure within each block contributes
\(\lfloor m/2\rfloor+1\) distinct eigenspaces. For odd \(m\), their
multiplicities are

\[
(1,\underbrace{2,\ldots,2}_{(m-1)/2}),
\]

whereas for even \(m\) they are

\[
(1,\underbrace{2,\ldots,2}_{m/2-1},1).
\]

Consequently, the multiplicity vector of the `BCS_CT` structure is

\[
\operatorname{qq}_{BCS\_CT}
=
(1,p-1)\otimes\operatorname{qq}_{CT,m}.
\]

For example, for \(p=3\) and \(m=7\),

```r
obj <- basis_BCS_CT(p = 3, m = 7)

obj$qq
```

returns

```r
[1] 1 2 2 2 2 4 4 4
```

since

\[
\operatorname{qq}_{CT,7}
=
(1,2,2,2),
\]

and hence

\[
(1, 2)\otimes(1,2,2,2) = (1,2,2,2,2,4,4,4).
\]

More generally, the first group of eigenspaces corresponds to the common direction across blocks, while the second group corresponds to between-block contrasts. Within each of these groups, the eigenspaces are further decomposed according to the circular Fourier-type eigenvectors within each block.

**Statistical interpretation:** The BCS_CT structure combines
exchangeability of the blocks with periodic dependence within each block. Specifically,

- the \(p\) blocks are exchangeable;
- the covariance structure between blocks is the same for every pair of distinct blocks;
- within each block, the covariance depends only on the circular
distance between variables;
- the between-block covariance also follows a circular Toeplitz
structure with respect to the within-block variables.

Thus, variables occupying corresponding positions in different blocks have the same between-block covariance, while within each block, variables separated by the same circular lag have the same covariance.

From the spectral point of view, the structure combines the
two-dimensional decomposition induced by block compound symmetry with the Fourier-type decomposition induced by circular Toeplitz structure. This gives a particularly natural representation for data possessing both exchangeable blocks and periodic structure within the blocks.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Repeated periodic measurements collected for several exchangeable subjects or experimental units.
> - Measurements over a cycle, such as hours of the day, days of the week, or months of the year, observed for several exchangeable groups.
> - Multisite or multilevel studies in which the measurement occasions have a natural circular ordering.
> - Periodic signals observed for several exchangeable experimental units, where both within-unit and between-unit covariance depend on circular lag.
> - Spatial or directional measurements collected for several
exchangeable locations or units.

## Block circular Toeplitz family

The block circular Toeplitz family assumes that the \(pm\)-dimensional
observation vector is partitioned into \(p\) subvectors (blocks) of
dimension \(m\),

\[
\mathbf y =
\left(
\mathbf y_1^\top,\ldots,\mathbf y_p^\top
\right)^\top,
\qquad
\mathbf y_i\in\mathbb R^m.
\]

The defining feature of block circular Toeplitz structure is that the
covariance structure between the blocks follows a circular Toeplitz
pattern. Thus, the covariance between two blocks depends only on their
circular distance. In contrast to block compound symmetry, different
circular distances may have different covariance matrices.

Let

\[
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0,\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1,\ldots,
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\lfloor p/2\rfloor}
\]

denote \(m\times m\) covariance matrices associated with the different circular distances between blocks. The covariance matrix then has the block-circular-Toeplitz form

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\operatorname{Toep}_{\mathrm{circ}}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0,
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1,\ldots,
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\lfloor p/2\rfloor},
\ldots,
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1
\right).
\]

Equivalently, it can be written as

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor p/2\rfloor}
\mathbf{SC}(p,k)\otimes\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_k,
\]

where \(\mathbf{SC}(p,k)\) is the symmetric circular matrix of order \(p\) having ones at circular distance \(k\).

Thus, the covariance matrix has the block form

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\left(
\begin{smallmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0 &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_2 &
\cdots &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1\\
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0 &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 &
\cdots &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_2\\
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_2 &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0 &
\cdots &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_3\\
\vdots &
\vdots &
\vdots &
\ddots &
\vdots\\
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_2 &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_3 &
\cdots &
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0
\end{smallmatrix}
\right),
\]

with the exact pattern determined by the circular distances between the blocks.

Consequently, the blocks are stationary with respect to cyclic
permutations: shifting all block indices by the same amount does not change the covariance matrix. In particular, the covariance between two blocks depends only on their circular separation and not on their absolute positions.

The spectral representation is especially useful for the block circular Toeplitz family. Let

\[
\mathbf H_{CT,p}
\]

denote the common orthonormal eigenbasis for \(p\times p\) circular Toeplitz matrices, as described in the *Circular Toeplitz* section. Let \(\mathbf V_i^{(p)}\) denote the projection matrices onto the corresponding eigenspaces. Then

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor p/2\rfloor+1}
\mathbf V_i^{(p)}\otimes\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i,
\]

where the matrices \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\) are linear combinations of the within-block covariance matrices,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i
=
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0
+
2\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor (p-1)/2\rfloor}
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_k
\cos\left(\frac{2\pi ik}{p}\right)
+
\begin{cases}
(-1)^i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{p/2}, & p\ \text{even},\\
0, & p\ \text{odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

The precise indexing of the eigenvalues follows the ordering of the basis returned by `basis_CT(p)`.

The construction used by `TestCQS` exploits the fact that the matrices \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\) inherit the same within-block covariance structure whenever all matrices
\(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_k\) belong to the same covariance family. Hence, the block and within-block decompositions can again be combined through a Kronecker product.

The four block circular Toeplitz structures implemented in the package are

| Structure | Within-block covariance structure | Generator |
| :-------- | :-------------------------------- | :-------- |
| `BCT_S`   | Sphericity                       | `basis_BCT_S(p,m)`  |
| `BCT_D`   | Diagonality                      | `basis_BCT_D(p,m)`  |
| `BCT_CS`  | Compound symmetry                | `basis_BCT_CS(p,m)` |
| `BCT_CT`  | Circular Toeplitz                | `basis_BCT_CT(p,m)` |

The corresponding basis matrices are obtained by combining the
block-level circular Toeplitz basis with the appropriate within-block basis,

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf H_{CT,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{\mathrm{within}}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf H_{BCT\_S}
  &= \mathbf H_{CT,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{S,m},\\
\mathbf H_{BCT\_D}
  &= \mathbf H_{CT,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{D,m},\\
\mathbf H_{BCT\_CS}
  &= \mathbf H_{CT,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{CS,m},\\
\mathbf H_{BCT\_CT}
  &= \mathbf H_{CT,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{CT,m}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The eigenvalue multiplicity vectors follow the same Kronecker-product principle. If \(\operatorname{qq}_{CT,p}\) denotes the multiplicity vector of the block circular Toeplitz structure and \(\operatorname{qq}_{W,m}\) the multiplicity vector of the selected within-block structure, then

\[
\operatorname{qq}_{BCT\_W}
=
\operatorname{qq}_{CT,p}\otimes
\operatorname{qq}_{W,m},
\]

for \(W\in\{S,D,CS,CT\}\).

For example, if \(p=7\), then

\[
\operatorname{qq}_{CT,7}=(1,2,2,2),
\]

so for a circular Toeplitz structure with compound symmetry within each block,

\[
\operatorname{qq}_{BCT\_CS}
=
(1,2,2,2)\otimes(1,m-1).
\]

This decomposition shows explicitly how the spectral structure is built in the two dimensions: the first factor describes the periodic relationship between blocks, while the second describes the covariance structure within each block.

The following subsections describe the four members of the block
circular Toeplitz family in detail.


### Block circular Toeplitz with spherical within-block structure (BCT_S)

The `BCT_S` structure is obtained when the within-block covariance
matrices are spherical. Thus,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_k=\tau_k\mathbf I_m,
\qquad
k=0,\ldots,\left\lfloor\frac p2\right\rfloor,
\]

where the coefficients \(\tau_k\) determine the circular Toeplitz covariance structure between the \(p\) blocks.

Consequently,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor p/2\rfloor}
\tau_k\,\mathbf{SC}(p,k)\otimes\mathbf I_m,
\]

or, equivalently,

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor p/2\rfloor+1}
\lambda_i
\left(\mathbf V_i\otimes\mathbf I_m\right),
\]

where \(\mathbf V_i\) are the block-level circular Toeplitz projection matrices and \(\lambda_i\) are the corresponding eigenvalues.

Since the within-block covariance is spherical, every block-level eigenvalue is repeated over all \(m\) within-block directions. Consequently,

\[
\operatorname{qq}_{BCT\_S}
=
\operatorname{qq}_{CT,p}\otimes(m).
\]

For example,

```r
obj <- basis_BCT_S(p = 7, m = 4)

obj$qq
```

returns

```text
[1] 4 8 8 8
```

because

\[
(1,2,2,2)\otimes(4)
=
(4,8,8,8).
\]

The corresponding basis matrix is

\[
\mathbf H
=
\mathbf H_{CT,p}\otimes\mathbf H_{S,m}
=
\mathbf H_{CT,p}\otimes\mathbf I_m.
\]

Thus, the circular Fourier-type eigenvectors describe the periodic relationship between the blocks, while the spherical within-block structure contributes \(m\) identical orthogonal directions.

**Statistical interpretation:** The `BCT_S` structure assumes that

- the covariance between blocks depends only on their circular distance,
- all variables within a block have the same variance,
- variables occupying different positions within a block are uncorrelated.

> **Typical applications**
>
> - Periodic or cyclic blocks with independent within-block variables.
